§!The City of Jerusalem, being the third holiest city in Islam, should reasonably be held by the stewards of the faith. However after the Uprising of 1811 Egypt retook the city from the Christian rebels, and have refused to return the land to us. They have now replied to our latest demand for its return with a total refusal. They say that the city was lost to rebels during our rule, and that a city such as Jerusalem needs stability to ensure the safe passage of those who go there on pilgrimages. This goes against the word of the Caliph, and is treason of the highest order. Yet the question is if a war with a muslim nation would serve the Islamic world well, even if said nation is defying our commands.§g

§!The City of Jerusalem, being the third holiest city in Islam, should reasonably be held by the stewards of the faith. However after the Uprising of 1811 Egypt retook the city from the Christian rebels, and have refused to return the land to us. They have now replied to our latest demand for its return with a proposal. They will be allowed to keep the lands of Jerusalem and Transjordan, and in return they will come to the aid of the Sultan Osman II of Rum in the war against Cappadocia. §REnsuring the victory of Rum is vital for Muslim control over Anatolia, yet we would have to give up our claim on Jerusalem to guarantee it. Rum might very well win the war without the help of Egypt, but knowing that we intervened on their behalf would surely help ensure the continued loyalty of the Sultanate.§!§g

§!The City of Jerusalem, being the third holiest city in Islam, should reasonably be held by the stewards of the faith. However after the Uprising of 1811 Egypt retook the city from the Christian rebels, and have refused to return the land to us. They have now replied to our latest demand with an explanation, stating that they have now ensured the region will remain stable under our control and that it will be returned with haste. The Caliph's word carries immense power, so it does not take much genius to understand that they are most likely trying to gain favor with the Caliph. Regardless of their intent, they have today shown themselves to be loyal servants, and we will of course always value those that are loyal to the true Caliph.§g
§!The Sultan of Rum has responded to our proposal. He has agreed to our demands and will now serve as our loyal governor of Anatolia.§g

§!The Sultan of Rum has responded to our proposal. He has refused our demands, saying that Rum will never be subjugated by another power. It is a shame, but it seems we are left with no choice but forcing his hand in the matter.§g

§!"The nations of the one true faith fight amongst ourselves whilst our people toil away endlessly. Hundreds of thousands of faithful men have died in our many wars, and for what purpose other than personal glory? The people deserve better, they do not wish for these wars, nor does Allah. The only ones who think these wars neccesary are petty rulers and despots, desperate to gain riches."\nThe Caliph speaks for a longtime, railing against the internal bickering occuring across the Islamic world. The shame felt in that room would stay with the delegates for the rest of their lives. The speech cuts deep, echoing the words spoken by qadi Abu-Saad al-Harawi 800 years ago.§g

§!"Whilst we wage war against one another, using the resources of the Christian world to win internal power struggles, we remain blind to what is happening. We keep entangling our nations deeper and deeper with the European markets, resources and militaries. So what, pray tell, will we do if the armies of Europe turn on us? When the Christians come to retake Jerusalem, will we be ready to stand united against them, or will we allow them to exploit these internal conflicts to their advantage, subjugating the Islamic world to their dominion? We must each look within ourselves and ask if we are ready for this conflict, for the Christians are clever and plotting and have been ever since the sixth crusade."\nThe Caliph's words cut deep. How can one claim to act for the benefit of Islam if ones actions will lead to its defeat?§g

§!"When the Prophet spread the faith across the middle east, do you believe he envisioned a future where his followers would fight over land and resources? That they would send thousands of men to the grave in the name of personal glory? Would he have fallen for such vain and petty temptations?"\nThe Caliph of Mecca speaks for a long time, pointing out the obvious failing of our many nations to work for the benefit of Islam and its followers. No one dares raise an objection to the speech, for we all know it to be true. What would the Prophet think if he saw the Islamic world today?§g

§!"To ensure the continued diversity of culture and thought that Islam has, we will ensure that the local nobility, judges, clerks, and bureaucrats remain people from the local areas. To go against this diversity would be to deny the will of Allah, as if he did not wish for us to have such broad diverse cultures he would not have made man as such."\nThe promise of allowing for the continued existance of local nobility and administrators are good to hear, and ensures that this union will not be one dominated by one group, be that cultural or political.§g

§!"To ensure the stability and unification of Islam some sacrifices will have to be made. The current feudal structure in many nations does not lend itself to benefitting the people, and as many of your lieges will know the resistance of the nobility to any kind of reform is a permanent issue in society. However, one cannot form a union consisting of so many people's and expect that the same law, reform or system will work equally well for all people. That is why we promise that administrators of all areas will be from each respective region, and given enough freedom to ensure that the people of each region is governed in the way that fit them best."\nThe Caliph continued speaking on the measures and legal structure of the union, but the main point was clear: this will be a union that includes all people in the nation, not simply a cultural or legal elite.§g

§!"The problems that our civilization faces is a result of our many different beliefs and cultures. To identify as being from Arabia, Egypt, or Rifia instead of simply saying 'I am a muslim' leads to these internal conflicts. The union cannot succeed if we do not combat the ills of nationalism at their core."\nThe Caliph spoke strongly in favour of the unification of not just our seperate political entities, but also of the legal and cultural structures across the Islamic world. To deny our people their unique culture is an obvious attempt to make the Arabians the stewards of all of Islam.§g

§!"The matter of monarchy is one that is complex. The people of Islam deserve representation and freedom, and how can that be achieved if monarchs rule over them via their blood? How could a union function with so many monarchs of different ranks and status all having the power to rule over their respective land? It could not, which is why the monarchy as an institution needs to be abolished. The lands and riches will be allowed to stay within the respective family, but the political power and titles will need to be abdicated willingly if we wish for the people of our nations to truly prosper."\nThe Caliph spoke for a long time arguing in favor of abolishing the different monarchies across the many nations represented at the congress. While it is true that this union would simply not work if we had 50 monarchs, one can also see an obvious incentive for the Caliph to hold this position. With the monarchs gone, political power would flow from the divine mandate given to the Caliph.§g

§!"We must seek further unity amongst our people. The casus belli for many conflicts across the Islamic world has had their roots in the lineage and dynasty of the many sultans, kings, and emperors across our vast civilization. The purpose of this congress is not to abolish monarchy, the monarchs do serve Allah as his shadow on this earth, administrating his laws and ensuring his will is realized. Thus, we instead aim to reform the monarchy. The monarchs will keep their titles, but serve a more ceremonial role. They will retain an important role in society, as when the Caliph must consider a new law and how it would impact our nation who would be better to ask than the monarchs, who know their people on a deeper level than most other people could ever dream of?"\nThe Caliph has called for a reform to the institution of monarchy, arguing that we can achieve a strong middleground between achieving political unity and republicanism.§g

§!"To seek the abolishment or reformation of the institution of monarchy would be a failure. Monarchs serve Allah in a special role as Zilullah fi'l-Ard, serving Allah as his legal administrators on Earth. While the Caliph will of course need to be accepted as being the leader of our nation, the monarchs will continue administrating their lands, continuing the good work they are already doing."\nThe Caliph spoke passionately about the strength and length of the ancient partnership between Sultan and Caliph. Both fulfill an important position in ensuring the will of Allah is achieved, and he argued that to threaten this relationship would be a grave mistake.§g

§!"The people and rulers following the Islamic faith have already recognized the truth of our words, and strength of our faith. The schizm was solved not just by us, but by the devout who recognized our legitimacy, be that those who always were loyal or those who realized the error of their ways. As such, we have shown the strength and power of our leadership, and you can rest assured that this union will be run by those who understand the importance of the faith."\nThe Caliph spoke passionately about the schizm and its resolution, and highlighted his role in ensuring stability and unity across our civilization.§g

§!"To deny the legitimacy of the Caliph of Mecca is to deny the will of the Prophet and Allah. If Mecca was not to be the center of Islam, then the Prophet would not have made it as such. Equally, had Allah not willed our rule He would not have granted us the strength and position we currently hold. We cannot expect a union of muslims to function if we allow such blatant cliffs to exist within society. There is but one true Caliph, and he rules Mecca."\nThe Caliph spoke lengthy about the importance of religious unity during these uncertain times, and obviously argued that it is with his leadership we can ensure that much needed unity.§g

§!"The diversity of thought, expression, and interpretation of the scripture is important if a religion wishes to stay modern and able to adapt to the issues of society. Thus we will encourage this diversity! However, for unity and order it is neccesary that one submits to a central leadership. Thus, we must also at the same time request that we rally behind one Caliph, who understands the importance and strength of differing interpretations."\nThe Caliph spoke about the importance of our many different interpretations of the word as written by the Prophet, but at the same time highlighted the importance of political unity.§g

§!The Caliph spoke briefly on the matter of the Schizm, but did not provide a solution to the problem. It seems in his desire to unite our many nations he has simply decided to pretend that the schizm does not exist.§g

§!"There are some in the Islamic world that would argue that the differences between Shia and Sunni muslims are as deep and wide as an ocean. While there are fundamental disagreements on several topics, we are all ultimately followers of the same god. To solve these disagreements is a noble and worthwhile task, and one that we will pursue with great ambition."\nThe Caliph argued for great ties to our Shia cousins, and forging a greater theological understanding for one another.§g

§!"While we disagree on many topics, some of them fundamental, Sunni and Shia muslims are more alike than we are different. To reject the idea of unity between our people over disputes that are, at their core, possible to remedy, would be foolish."\nThe Caliph made a lenthy speech, arguing that the differences between us and our Shia cousins are able to be resolved with limited efforts. They will not be granted any major concessions, but with many minor ones the differences can be solved.§g

§!"To deny the legitimacy of the Caliph is to deny the will of the Prophet and Allah! There will be no unity possible between those who deny the fundamental truth of the legitimate Caliph of Mecca and those who are faithful!"\nThe Caliph passionately ranted about how the Shia believers are unfaithful, and have disgraced themselves by straying from the word of the Prophet. It seems any attempt at resolving our differences will be in vain.§g
